catalog_quote: Gwara has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. The basic conventions are as follows; [table: High ʹ / Mid Unmarked / Low ˋ / Rising ˇ / Falling ˆ] All syllables are marked for tone in the present document. Thus any unmarked syllables should be assumed to be mid. A number of words exhibit three tone heights in one word, illustrating the contrast. Examples; Doctor nɛ́ragɔ̀w / Masquerade náŋgbaʒì / Thigh ìgyɔ́ŋda. Falling tone is very important and is often a significant marker of plurals in nouns. E.g; Housefly ìdzù ídzû / Chicken ìnù ínû / Cow ìnà ínâ. Rising tone is much rarer, but is present; Sheep ìdòy ídǒy ... [p. 7, Orthography:] Tone plays a crucial role in Gwara and it is difficult to see how an effective orthography could ignore this. Numerous plurals are made only by tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only prosodic description is tonal: three level tones (high, mid, low) plus rising and falling glides on every syllable, with tone also marking noun plurals. Stress is not mentioned at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author notes the transcription is preliminary (one elicitation session, 20 April 2009) and the draft is marked 'not for citation without reference to the author'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on citation forms from a wordlist; no phrase-level or sentence prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Gwara (autonym iGwara; Hausa 'Gora') of villages Gora A-E, Jaba and Kagarko LGAs, Kaduna State, Nigeria; Koro cluster, NW Plateau, closest to Idũ/Dũya (idun1241). Blench states it is NOT the 'Idon-Gora-Ankwe' of Crozier & Blench 1992. Matches gwar1240 exactly; no ISO code. Under 3,000 speakers, threatened.

sources.quote: Gwara has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. [...] All syllables are marked for tone in the present document. Thus any unmarked syllables should be assumed to be mid. A number of words exhibit three tone heights in one word, illustrating the contrast. sources.note: Nothing about stress. Section 3 Phonology (pp. 2-5) covers vowels, consonants and 3.3 Tones: three level tones (H, M, L) plus rising and falling glides, every syllable tone-marked; tonal plurals. The words stress/accent/prominence/intonation/pitch do not occur anywhere in the 27-page text layer. Data are from one elicitation session (20 Apr 2009, Gora A); transcription called preliminary.
